records.current_summary:
Guatemala demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: Asociación Lambda's observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022 — hundreds of incidents and dozens of deaths — with 35 victims saying they intended to flee the country. Guatemalan officials have explicitly excluded trans women from femicide-law protection on the grounds they are not “biological women.” There is no legal gender recognition and no SOGI hate-crime statute (a 2022 law actually increased penalties for “aggravated” LGBT visibility before being struck down).

Congress has repeatedly advanced anti-LGBT initiatives (Law 5276, the 2022 “Life and Family Protection” bill, later shelved after protests). The community is organised (a local group such as Lambda, plus trans collectives) but under pressure. Tourist areas (Antigua, Atitlán) are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from the general violence level.

prison_adds.title: Every Day I Live in Fear: Violence and Discrimination Against LGBT People in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, and Obstacles to Asylum in the United States (Human Rights Watch)
prison_adds.summary: HRW (7 Oct 2020), Guatemala chapter: 'Guatemalan authorities facilitate anti-trans violence is by placing trans women in men's prisons, exposing them to violence, including sexual assault.' Bárbara Herrarte, trans activist with Redmmutrans (Red Multicultural de Mujeres Trans), described her time in a men's prison: 'Always, at night, someone got in my bed and forced me to have sex with him.' Documents birth-sex placement in the men's prison system as of 2020 with sexual-assault risk, and no gender-identity-based placement policy, special trans unit, or trans-specific solitary/segregation practice; LGBTQ org Lambda flags forced internal displacement from violence generally, but no trans-specific custody-policy or court ruling is documented in the report.

records.current_summary: South Korea is broadly workable for trans visitors — there is no criminalisation, courts have protected trans people's restroom access and ruled favourably on legal gender recognition, and Seoul hosts one of Asia's largest Pride parades. There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner, and no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering services. No severe incidents involving trans visitors are documented. Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are welcoming; outside them, more caution is warranted.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in South Korea (Wikipedia)
prison_adds.summary: One Wikipedia full-text search round surfaced no dedicated article on trans prisoners in South Korea; the jurisdiction's LGBTQ-rights article documents its only prominent trans-in-state-placement case, military rather than civilian: Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, a transgender conscript, was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical/mental handicap; she died by suicide in March 2021; the Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021; and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty. The same article records that consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel is criminalised under Military Criminal Act article 92-6 (up to two years' imprisonment; a gay soldier was sentenced to six months in 2017) and that transgender people are excluded from military service. It contains no information on how transgender prisoners are housed in South Korea's civilian prison system - no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, special unit, or solitary/segregation practice is described. (Last-resort encyclopedic source; fetched and verified.)

records.current_summary:
Mexico pairs meaningful legal progress with one of the world's highest tolls of violence against transgender people. Twenty-two of its 32 states offer administrative legal gender recognition, Mexico City and Nayarit have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections exist.

Against that, 71 trans or gender-diverse people were murdered in a single recent year — the second-highest figure in the Americas after Brazil — with organised crime increasingly involved and impunity near-total. The victims are overwhelmingly local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit, not tourists; violence is also highly concentrated by region.

In major tourist destinations and central Mexico City, heavily policed and progressively governed, a trans visitor's everyday risk is closer to harassment than violence. The dominant hazard for any traveller is Mexico's general crime environment. Use the Admin Divisions view: state-level scores range from among Latin America's best (Mexico City) to levels comparable with its most dangerous regions.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ people in prison (Wikipedia; Mexico section)
prison_adds.summary: Thin: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ people in prison' article, Mexico section, records only one Mexico-specific policy: in July 2007, through the efforts of the National Human Rights Commission (CDHDF), the Mexico City prison system began allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, with visitors not required to be married to the inmate, applying to all Mexico City prisons. The article contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement (birth-sex vs identity placement), special units, or solitary/segregation practice for Mexico.

records.current_summary:
Greece is a workable destination with a clear law-versus-practice gap. The legal framework is among Europe's strongest — it ranks 7th on the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map, has banned conversion therapy and intersex infant surgery, has a hate-crime law covering gender identity, and legalised same-sex marriage in 2024 (the first Orthodox-majority country to do so). There are no trans-specific border or bathroom restrictions, and the government is progressive with an improving trajectory.

But the social reality lags the law. A mob of about 150 people assaulted two trans people in Thessaloniki; an European Court of Human Rights case documented police detention and mistreatment of trans sex workers; surveys show Greeks are markedly more avoidant of public LGBTI visibility than the EU average (63% avoid holding hands); and the UK Foreign Office has issued an LGBTQ travel warning for Greece.

Major tourist destinations — Mykonos, Athens's Gazi district, Thessaloniki — are welcoming; outside them the climate is rougher than the law suggests.

prison_adds.title: Φυλακές Κορυδαλλού: Τρανς κρατούμενες θα μεταχθούν για πρώτη φορά στη γυναικεία πτέρυγα (LiFO)
prison_adds.summary: LiFO (4 Dec 2021): four trans detainees were ordered transferred to the women's prisons of Korydallou (Athens) by decision of the General Secretary for Crime-Prevention Policy Sofia Nikolaou, after each had petitioned for transfer stating they identify and wish to be treated as women. The four (three Greek, one Bulgarian) had been held at Trikala and Corfu prisons, effectively isolated and treated inconsistently with their self-identified gender. First documented transfer of trans prisoners to a women's facility in Greece; it illustrates that default placement had followed the male facilities and that an on-request transfer route to women's facilities existed.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Greece — Correctional Facilities section (Wikipedia)
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia's overview of Greek LGBTQ rights records under 'Correctional Facilities' that since 4 December 2021 trans women detainees, upon their request, may be relocated to correctional facilities for women — the policy change matching the Korydallou transfers reported by LiFO the same day. Placement thus starts from the registered sex, with a 4 Dec 2021 decision creating an on-request transfer route for trans women; the article documents no special trans units and no rule covering trans men's placement.

records.current_summary:
Nigeria is among the most severe environments for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the SSMPA (14 years, applies to all including tourists), and 12 northern states apply Sharia law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct. A transgender TikToker known as "Abuja Area Mama" was found beaten and dead on a highway in Abuja; police misgendered her in death and, six months later, no one has been arrested. Police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for "looking gay" — the SSMPA has been described as a "weaponised" law — and dating-app "kito" gangs use Grindr to lure victims into assault and robbery. The UK Foreign Office has warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks.

A proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public. Trans identity is NOT explicitly criminalized nationally (the SSMPA targets same-sex conduct), and the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists. But the Sharia death penalty, the trans-specific killing with impunity, the police brutality, and the UK advisory make this an environment to avoid entirely.

prison_adds.title: Bobrisky — Wikipedia (Nigerian transgender woman; 2024 imprisonment at Kirikiri)
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia biography of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, documents the only trans-imprisonment case the search surfaced: she pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine. She served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, and was released on 5 August 2024. At sentencing, press coverage (BBC Pidgin, cited in the article) openly asked 'which prison they will keep the crossdresser in', reflecting discretionary placement; the article does not record whether she was assigned to a male or female section. Outcome/ruling: an October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
